topic.examWeightHint: Unit 2 is one hour and fifty marks over six questions, sat every Summer. F = ma along a level floor had a question of its own in 2019, 2022 and 2023, Q3 each time and 7 to 9 marks, each time with a pull at an angle to the floor and in 2022 with a friction per kilogram as well; in the other years it is one step inside a connected-bodies or slope question. Expect the normal reaction, the acceleration and a follow-on part, with the equation of motion carrying the method marks and the mass-for-weight slip costing the rest.
mustMemorise: F in F = ma is the resultant force along the line of motion
The m is the mass in kilograms; the weight mg in newtons goes on the diagram
Friction is given as a value or as a value per kilogram — multiply a per-kilogram rate by the mass
Choose a positive direction, write it down, and take the resultant in it
For a lift, up positive gives T - mg = ma
A pull P at θ above a level floor: P cos θ drives, and R = mg - P sin θ
Constant velocity means no acceleration: the forces along the line of motion balance
A 'show that' is derived forwards; verifying by substitution is capped at two marks

Momentum, impulse and collisions; Newton's third law as a named law with action-reaction pairs
Air resistance modelled as a function of speed, and terminal velocity

sheet.howExamined: Unit 2, one hour, fifty marks, six questions, calculator allowed, formula sheet on page 2, g = 10 m/s² on the front page. When this has a question of its own it is a block on a level floor: Summer 2019 Q3 (a string at an angle on a smooth table: the diagram, the reaction, the acceleration, a speed), Summer 2022 Q3 (a 'show that' with friction per kilogram, then a second box on a string at an angle, with the pull to find) and Summer 2023 Q3 (a pull at an angle: the reaction, the friction at a steady speed, then a new pull and friction). In other years F = ma is one step inside a connected-bodies or slope question. Schemes are in MW and W: one mark for the resultant, one for = ma, then the value, with follow-through throughout.
traps: The acceleration multiplied by the weight instead of the mass (Summer 2019 Q3(iii))
The normal reaction written as the pull's upward part alone, a two-term vertical equation, or the vertical balance never set up (Summer 2019 Q3(ii))
The reaction given as the whole weight with no resolving, or as the pull's upward part (Summer 2023 Q3(i))
An acceleration looked for when the block moves at a constant velocity (Summer 2023 Q3(ii))

A 'show that' worked backwards from the printed acceleration, which scored nothing (Summer 2022 Q3(a))
A resistance given as so many newtons per kilogram not multiplied by the mass (Summer 2022 Q3(b)(i))
The mass not changed in the equation after the load changes (Summer 2022 Q3(b)(ii))
A 'show that' verified by substitution, which is capped at two marks (Summer 2024 Q6(ii))
Weights used as masses, or masses as forces, in F = ma (Summer 2025 Q4(ii))
The weight left out of a vertical equation, so the tension alone is divided by the mass
The acceleration arrow drawn as though it were one of the forces

steps.working: For the box, taking the direction of motion as positive:
steps.decision: Name the body and the direction before any numbers. Examiners report forces on one body confused with forces on a whole system, and this line is what prevents it.

options: Because F = ma applies to one named body, and the forces must be that body's own
Because it is the conventional way to lay out the page
Because the direction of motion is always to the right
whyMenu.explain: A resultant only means something once you have said which body it acts on and which way you are calling positive. Both change the signs in the next line.

steps.decision: $F$ in $F = ma$ is the resultant along the line of motion, not one of the forces. Write the subtraction out so the resistance is visibly taken off.
The $m$ is the mass in kilograms. The $70$ N on the diagram is the weight, and it plays no part here because the box is not moving vertically.

steps.decision: The diagram needs the weight in newtons, so convert the mass once and write it on the arrow. This is the only place the two meet.

options: Because a force diagram is drawn in newtons, and a mass in kilograms is not a force
Because the mass must be converted before it can go into F = ma
Because weight and mass are two words for the same quantity

steps.decision: State the positive direction, then write the resultant in that direction. The cable pulls up and gravity pulls down, so the resultant is the difference.
The answer is positive, and up was positive, so the acceleration is upwards. Say so: a direction is part of the answer here.

workedExamples.stem:
A block of mass 5 kg is pulled along a rough horizontal floor by a rope at 30° above the horizontal. The tension in the rope is 40 N and the friction on the block is 12 N.

(i) Calculate the normal reaction of the floor on the block.
(ii) Calculate the acceleration of the block.

Take $g = 10$ m/s². Round to 2 decimal places.

steps.working:
Along the floor: $40\cos 30° = 34.64$ N
Upwards: $40\sin 30° = 20$ N
steps.decision: The rope is the only force at an angle, so it is the only one to resolve. The cosine is the part next to the angle, along the floor; the sine is the part opposite it, straight up.

options: Because the rope pulls partly along the floor and partly upwards, and each direction gets its own equation
Because every force in a mechanics question has to be resolved
Because the weight acts at an angle to the floor
whyMenu.explain: The weight, the reaction and the friction already lie along the two directions that matter. Only the rope does not, so only the rope is split.

steps.working:
Vertically the block does not accelerate:
$R + 20 = 50$
$R = 30$ N
steps.decision: Nothing moves up or down, so the upward forces balance the downward one. The rope's upward part carries 20 N of the weight, so the floor carries only the rest.

steps.working:
Along the floor, direction of motion positive:
$34.64 - 12 = 5a$
steps.decision: Only the rope's part along the floor drives the block, and the friction opposes it. The resultant goes equal to the mass times the acceleration.
Divide by the mass, 5 kg, not the weight, and give the answer to 2 decimal places, as the stem asks.

items.stem: From an earlier topic: a body has a mass of 6 kg. What is its weight, taking $g = 10$ m/s²?

options.feedback: Weight $= mg = 6 \times 10 = 60$ N.
That is the mass with a newton sign on it. Multiply by $g$ to turn a mass into a force.
That divides by $g$. Weight is the mass multiplied by $g$.
That is the mass again. A weight is a force, measured in newtons.

items.stem: From an earlier topic: rearrange $F = ma$ to make $a$ the subject.

options.feedback: $m$ is multiplying $a$, so divide both sides by $m$.
The fraction is upside down. Dividing both sides by $m$ leaves $F$ on top.
$ma$ is a product, so $m$ cannot be removed by subtracting it.
Multiplying by $m$ undoes nothing; it is division that clears it.

items.stem: From an earlier topic: a rope costs 4 pounds per metre. What do 8 metres cost?

options.feedback: $4 \times 8 = 32$: a rate per unit is multiplied by the number of units.
That is the cost of one metre. Eight metres cost eight times as much.
That divides instead of multiplying.
That adds the two numbers. A rate per unit is multiplied.

items.skill: Mass or weight in F = ma
items.stem: A box of mass 5 kg, weight 50 N, is pushed by a resultant force of 30 N. What is its acceleration?

options.feedback: $30 = 5a$, so $a = 6$ m/s². The $m$ in $F = ma$ is the mass in kilograms.
That divides by the weight, 50 N. The weight belongs on the diagram, not in the equation.
That multiplies instead of dividing. $F = ma$ rearranges to $a = F \div m$.
That subtracts one number from the other. The relationship is a product, not a difference.

items.stem: A body is pushed by 60 N against a resistance of 20 N. Which number goes into $F = ma$?

options.feedback: $F$ is the resultant along the line of motion: $60 - 20 = 40$ N.
That is the driving force alone. The resistance is still acting, so it comes off first.
The resistance opposes the motion, so it is subtracted rather than added.
That is the resistance alone, which acts backwards.

items.stem: A resistance of 5 N per kg acts on a body of mass 9 kg. What is the resisting force?

options.feedback: $5 \times 9 = 45$ N: every kilogram is resisted by 5 N.
That is the force on one kilogram. Multiply by the mass to get the whole force.
That divides the mass by the rate. A rate per kilogram is multiplied by the mass.
That divides the other way round, and a force needs a unit.

items.stem: A lift of mass 300 kg hangs on a cable with tension 3300 N. Taking up as positive and $g = 10$ m/s², which equation is right?

options.feedback: The resultant upwards is the tension minus the weight, and the weight is $300 \times 10 = 3000$ N.
The weight is still acting. Leaving it out is the commonest slip on a vertical problem.
The weight acts downwards while the tension acts upwards, so they subtract.
That subtracts the mass rather than the weight. A force diagram is in newtons.

parts.workedSolution: Taking up as positive, $3600 - 4000 = 400a$ gives $a = -1$ m/s². The minus sign means the acceleration is 1 m/s² downwards, so its magnitude is 1 m/s².

commonErrors.feedback: That is the tension divided by the mass, with the weight missing. The lift's weight is 4000 N and it never switches off.

A lift and its passengers have a total mass of $M$ kg. The lift hangs on a vertical cable in which the tension is 7020 N, and it accelerates upwards at 0.8 m/s².

Show that $M = 650$.

Take $g = 10$ m/s².

accepted: Taking up as positive, 7020 - 10M = 0.8M, so 7020 = 10.8M and M = 650.

parts.stem:
A crate of mass 4 kg is dragged along a rough, level floor by a rope that pulls with 25 N at 30° above the horizontal.

Calculate the normal reaction between the crate and the floor.

Take $g = 10$ m/s².

Answer ________ N
hints: Nothing moves up or down, so the vertical forces balance.
The rope's upward part shares the weight with the floor.
parts.workedSolution: Vertically: $R + 25\sin 30° = 40$, so $R + 12.5 = 40$ and $R = 27.5$ N.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the whole weight, with no resolving. The rope pulls partly upwards, so the floor carries less: $R = 40 - 25\sin 30°$.
That is the rope's upward part on its own. The vertical balance has three forces in it: $R + 12.5 = 40$.
That takes off $25\cos 30°$, the part along the floor. The balance is right, so the mark (M) stands; the upward part is the sine.

parts.stem:
The crate moves at a constant velocity.

Calculate the friction acting on the crate.

Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer ________ N

scheme.for: $25\cos 30° - F = 0$ (no acceleration, so the forces along the floor balance)

hints: Constant velocity means no acceleration.
So the rope's part along the floor and the friction balance.
parts.workedSolution: No acceleration, so along the floor $F = 25\cos 30° = 21.65$ N.

commonErrors.feedback: That is $25\sin 30°$, the rope's upward part. The friction balances the part along the floor, which is the cosine; the balance itself earns the mark (M).
That balances the friction against the whole 25 N. Only the part of the rope along the floor, $25\cos 30°$, pulls against the friction.

parts.stem:
The rope is changed for a stronger pull of 36 N at 40° above the horizontal, and the friction becomes 14 N.

Calculate the acceleration of the crate.

Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer ________ m/s²
hints: A new pull and a new friction: build the equation again.
Only the new rope's part along the floor drives the crate.
parts.workedSolution: Along the floor: $36\cos 40° - 14 = 4a$, so $27.58 - 14 = 4a$ and $a = 3.39$ m/s².

commonErrors.feedback: That uses $36\sin 40°$ along the floor. The $= 4a$ mark (M) stands; the part along the floor is the cosine.
That uses the whole 36 N along the floor. The rope is at 40°, so only $36\cos 40°$ drives the crate.
That divides by the weight, 40 N. The resultant is right, so both method marks (M) stand; $F = ma$ takes the mass, 4 kg.

findTheMistake.stem: Eoin is finding the acceleration of a 7 kg box pulled by 40 N against a resistance of 12 N, with $g = 10$ m/s². His working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 4 puts the weight, 70 N, where $F = ma$ wants the mass. The weight is the right number for the downward arrow on the diagram, and line 3 works it out correctly, but it has no place in the equation of motion. Using it makes the acceleration ten times too small.
findTheMistake.feedback: Naming the body and forming the resultant are both right, and they earn the two method marks (M). The habit that fixes the last line is to write the unit beside every number as you use it: kilograms go into the equation, newtons go on the diagram.

findTheMistake.stem: Niall is finding the normal reaction on a box of mass 5.5 kg pulled along a smooth, level floor by a string at 35° above the horizontal, with a tension of 16 N and $g = 10$ m/s². His working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 2 makes the reaction equal to the string's upward part, as if the floor only had to balance the string. Vertically there are three forces: the reaction and the string's upward part together hold up the 55 N weight, so $R + 16\sin 35° = 55$.
findTheMistake.feedback: The weight is right and so is the choice of sine for the upward part, which earns the resolving mark (M). Before writing the vertical line, list every force with an up or down part and put all of them in it: a two-term equation here is the slip the reports keep finding.

findTheMistake.stem: A crate of mass 10 kg pushed by 75 N against a resistance of 3 N per kg accelerates at 4.5 m/s². A 5 kg box is then put on the crate and they move together, with the same 75 N push and the same 3 N per kg. Aisling's working for the new acceleration:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 3 has the old mass, 10 kg, on the right-hand side. Lines 1 and 2 already use the new mass for the resistance, but the $ma$ must use it too: the 30 N resultant now has 15 kg to accelerate.
findTheMistake.feedback: The new mass and the new resistance are both right, and so is the resultant: those earn the method marks (M). When a part changes the body, rewrite the equation from the start with the new mass in every place it appears, not only where the question points to it.

prompts.prompt: What does the $F$ in $F = ma$ stand for?
prompts.answer: The resultant force along the line of motion, not any single force acting.

prompts.prompt: Which of a body's two numbers goes into $F = ma$, the mass or the weight?
prompts.answer: The mass, in kilograms. The weight in newtons goes on the force diagram.

prompts.prompt: A resistance is given as 4 N per kg. How do you turn it into a force?
prompts.answer: Multiply it by the mass of the body, on its own line of working.

prompts.prompt: Why does CCEA never ask you for a coefficient of friction?
prompts.answer: Because $F = \mu R$ is excluded from this specification: friction is always given as a value, or as a value per unit mass.

prompts.prompt: What is the first line to write for a lift on a cable?
prompts.answer: The positive direction, then the resultant: the tension minus the weight equals the mass times the acceleration.

prompts.prompt: What does a 'show that' part want, and what does verifying cost?
prompts.answer: It wants the equation formed from the forces and solved forwards; substituting the printed answer back in is capped at two marks.

prompts.prompt: A later part increases the load. What has to change in the equation?
prompts.answer: The mass, because the body is heavier now; re-read the part and rebuild the equation before solving.

prompts.prompt: A box on a level floor is pulled by a rope at $\theta$ above the horizontal with tension $P$. What is the normal reaction?
prompts.answer: The weight take away the rope's upward part: $R = mg - P\sin\theta$, because the rope and the floor share the job of holding the box up.

prompts.prompt: A block is dragged along a floor at a constant velocity. What is the resultant force on it?
prompts.answer: Zero: there is no acceleration, so the forces along the floor balance and the pull's part along it equals the friction.

prompts.prompt: A box on a level floor is pulled by a rope at $\theta$ above the horizontal with tension $P$. What is its normal reaction?
prompts.answer: $R = mg - P\sin\theta$: the weight minus the rope's upward part.
